blocks.text: **Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL)** is a _clonal_ disorder of **small, mature-looking B lymphocytes**. The cells look normal but are **functionally incompetent**: they do not transform or make antibody when they meet antigen. Because the clone keeps growing without doing useful work, a large mass of immunologically useless cells builds up in blood, marrow, nodes, spleen and liver. It is an **indolent, incurable** disease of older people.

**Chronic vs acute leukaemia:** in a chronic leukaemia the malignant clone can still differentiate, so _mature_ cells pile up. In an acute leukaemia primitive **blasts** accumulate and quickly cause marrow failure.

blocks.title: CLL and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL): one disease
items: The tumour cells of CLL and SLL cannot be told apart, and both are treated the same way; the WHO classification counts them as **one entity at different stages**.
**CLL**: leukaemic picture, with the clone in blood above **5 × 10^9/L (5000/µL)**.
**SLL**: mainly nodal (localised) disease, with fewer than 5 × 10^9/L clonal cells in blood but lymphadenopathy ± splenomegaly.
**Monoclonal B lymphocytosis (MBL)**: a CLL-type clone that falls short of the CLL criteria (no qualifying count, no nodal disease); managed by observation.

blocks.title: Epidemiology at a glance
rows: Commonest leukaemia — about **30%** of all cases
Davidson 30%; Kumar, Pocket and Step-Up also call it the commonest
Median **65–70 years** at presentation; rises steeply with age
Strikingly **rare in Chinese** and related populations
Most marked geographical variation of any leukaemia
CLL is the largest single group

blocks.text: Exam age clue for leukaemia type: **ALL** under 13 years, **AML** 13–40, **CML** 40–60, **CLL** over 60.
Quoted median ages differ between books (65 to 71 years). Use **Davidson’s 65–70 years** and remember that CLL is the leukaemia of older adults.

For most leukaemias **no cause is found**. General leukaemia risk factors are **ionising radiation**, **cytotoxic drugs** (especially alkylating agents) and industrial **benzene**, **retroviruses** (HTLV-1), **genetic factors** (identical twin of an affected patient, Down’s syndrome) and **immune deficiency** such as hypogammaglobulinaemia. None of these is specific to CLL.

In Davidson’s risk-factor box, radiation and alkylating agents are tied mainly to **myeloid** leukaemia and HTLV-1 to **adult T-cell** leukaemia/lymphoma. Do not pick them as a recognised cause of CLL.

blocks.title: Monoclonal B lymphocytosis — the precursor state
items: Almost every case of CLL is preceded by **MBL**: a circulating clonal B-cell population **below 5 × 10^9/L**.
MBL is common — present in about **12% of healthy people** — and most never progress.
Its relation to CLL mirrors that of **MGUS to myeloma**.
**High-count MBL** (clone above 0.5 × 10^9/L) should be separated from low-count MBL: review **at least yearly** for progression and infection risk.

blocks.title: How the disease produces its effects
items: **Failed maturation:** the clonal cells do not become antibody-secreting plasma cells → **hypogammaglobulinaemia** and infections.
**Marrow crowding:** infiltration displaces normal haematopoiesis → anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia.
**Low growth fraction:** neoplasms of mature cells divide slowly, so the course runs over many years.
**B-cell receptor (BCR) signalling:** CLL cells depend on abnormal, persistent BCR pathway signals; **Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK)** and **PI3 kinase** are links in that pathway.
**Blocked apoptosis:** the anti-apoptotic protein **BCL-2** is abnormally active in CLL cells.
**Recurrent mutations:** TP53, NOTCH1, MYD88 and SF3B1; spliceosome mutations are thought to play a key role.

blocks.title: Pathway targets and the drugs that hit them

blocks.text: Think **MBL : CLL = MGUS : myeloma** — a common, mostly harmless clone that is the soil from which the malignancy grows.

Onset is **insidious**. In about **70%** of patients CLL is found _by chance_ when a full blood count done for another reason shows a lymphocytosis. Symptoms, when they come, reflect **immune failure**, **marrow failure** and **lymphoid enlargement**; systemic symptoms usually appear later in the course.

blocks.title: Symptoms and signs with their mechanism
rows: Low immunoglobulins and functional leucopenia, ± neutropenia
In about **80%**; often cervical; one area or generalised
In about **50%**; spleen may be massive → left upper quadrant discomfort
B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fever)
In **10–20%**; mostly later in the disease

blocks.text: Classic exam picture: an **older adult** with a **raised lymphocyte count**, small **painless nodes** and perhaps a palpable spleen, often with a history of **repeated chest or skin infections**.

**Hairy cell leukaemia** also gives cytopenias and splenomegaly, but **lymphadenopathy is rare**. **Prolymphocytic leukaemia** gives **massive splenomegaly with little lymphadenopathy**. Prominent nodes favour CLL.

The diagnosis is made on **peripheral blood**: a **mature lymphocytosis above 5 × 10^9/L** with typical morphology **plus** a characteristic **immunophenotype** on flow cytometry. A bone marrow examination is **not needed** to diagnose CLL.

blocks.title: Work-up of suspected CLL
rows: Raised WCC (often 50–200 × 10^9/L, can be far higher) with lymphocytosis; Hb and platelets normal or low
Small, mature, normal-looking lymphocytes; **smudge cells**; no blasts
Monoclonal B cells: **CD19, CD20, CD23** plus the aberrant T-cell marker **CD5**; one light chain only (**kappa or lambda**); dim surface Ig
**Hypogammaglobulinaemia** is common and worsens with time
**17p deletion or TP53 mutation** — essential before any treatment because it changes drug choice
Not required; helps in difficult cases, for prognosis (diffuse infiltration is adverse) and to judge response

blocks.text: **Smudge (smear) cells** are fragile CLL lymphocytes squashed while the film is being spread. They are an artefact, but a classic visual clue to CLL.

TP53 mutation is present in **under 10%** at diagnosis but in about **30% at relapse**, so a normal result at diagnosis does not hold for ever; Davidson advises testing **every patient before therapy starts**.

blocks.title: Differential diagnosis of a lymphocytosis
items: **Infection**: viral, or bacterial such as _Bordetella pertussis_ (polyclonal on flow).
**Lymphoproliferative disease**: CLL, lymphoma.
**After splenectomy**.
Immunophenotyping is what separates a **reactive** lymphocytosis from a clonal one.

blocks.text: A CLL-phenotype clone **below 5 × 10^9/L** without nodal disease is **monoclonal B lymphocytosis**, not CLL. (First Aid prints a B-cell threshold of “>500/mm³”; Davidson, Kumar and Pocket all use **5 × 10^9/L = 5000/µL** — use that.)
An **M protein** does not prove myeloma: about **5%** of CLL patients have a monoclonal gammopathy, and MGUS, lymphoma, Waldenström’s and amyloidosis can all produce one.
Lab contrast: **CLL = lymphocytosis** (B cells); **CML = granulocytosis** (neutrophils, myelocytes, eosinophils, basophils).

blocks.note: Look at: sheets of small mature lymphocytes with **smudge cells** (arrowed) — the classic CLL blood film.
Look at: FISH nuclei — panel A (green 17p probe, red 11q probe) shows the 17p (TP53) deletion with normal 11q; panel B shows three chromosome 12 signals (trisomy 12).

blocks.text: CLL is staged **clinically** — from examination of node areas, liver and spleen, plus the blood count. Stage predicts survival and guides when to treat. Davidson uses an **A/B/C clinical staging** (the Binet scheme); Kumar also gives the **Rai** system.

blocks.title: Davidson / Binet clinical staging
rows: No anaemia or thrombocytopenia; **fewer than 3** lymphoid areas enlarged
No anaemia or thrombocytopenia; **3 or more** areas enlarged
**Anaemia and/or thrombocytopenia**, whatever the number of areas

blocks.title: Rai staging (lymphocytosis present at every stage)

blocks.text: For Binet, the **five lymphoid areas** are cervical, axillary and inguinal nodes, **spleen** and **liver**. Cytopenias automatically make it stage C (Rai III/IV).

blocks.title: Biological prognostic markers
rows: **del 17p / TP53 mutation** (powerful marker; poor response to chemo-immunotherapy)
**Unmutated IGHV** (median ~8 years); ZAP70 expression tracks this
High **CD38**; **NOTCH1** or **SF3B1** mutation; diffuse marrow infiltration

blocks.text: Advanced stage (**Rai III/IV, Binet C**) counts as **active disease** and is an indication to treat. Among treatment triggers, **thrombocytopenia carries the worst prognosis**.
Do not mix the systems: **splenomegaly** is a defining feature of Rai II, but in Binet the spleen is just **one of five areas**. Anaemia means Rai III but Binet C.

CLL is the **least aggressive leukaemia**. Median survival is about **10 years**, and most **stage A** patients have a **normal life expectancy**; many die of something else. About **30% never need treatment**. Outlook depends on stage, age, pace (lymphocyte doubling time) and especially **TP53 status**; advanced disease more often kills through progression or infection. With chemotherapy plus rituximab about **90% are alive at 4 years**.

blocks.title: When to treat (otherwise watch and wait)
items: **Marrow failure** — worsening anaemia or thrombocytopenia not caused by autoimmunity.
**Massive or progressive** lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly.
**Systemic symptoms**: weight loss, night sweats, fever.
**Rapidly rising lymphocyte count** — Kumar: doubling in **under 6 months**.
**Autoimmune haemolysis or thrombocytopenia** responding poorly to steroids.
Recurrent infections; advanced stage (**Rai III/IV, Binet C**). Davidson notes that those treated are mainly **progressive stage A** and **stages B and C**.

blocks.text: **Early, stable disease:** no specific treatment. Explain the indolent nature of CLL and reassure — the word “leukaemia” frightens patients — and repeat the blood count every **3–6 months**.

blocks.title: Specific treatment (Davidson 24e framework)
rows: Anti-CD20 antibody + gentler chemotherapy: **bendamustine** or oral **chlorambucil**; **obinutuzumab + chlorambucil** beats rituximab + chlorambucil
Switch to a drug with a different mechanism
Non-myeloablative **allogeneic stem cell transplant** — the only potentially curative option

blocks.title: Supportive care
items: Transfusion for symptomatic anaemia or thrombocytopenia; erythropoietin may cut transfusion needs.
**Glucocorticoids** for autoimmune haemolysis or ITP (also for some marrow failure).
Treat infections promptly; prophylaxis during chemotherapy — antibacterial, antiviral (HSV/VZV), anti-_Pneumocystis_, antifungal.
**Immunoglobulin replacement** for hypogammaglobulinaemia with recurrent infections.
Vaccinate against **pneumococcus, Hib and influenza**; **avoid live vaccines**.
**Radiotherapy** for bulky or obstructing nodes or a painful spleen; **splenectomy** for autoimmune cytopenias, hypersplenism or massive splenomegaly.
**Allopurinol** to prevent hyperuricaemia when treatment starts.

blocks.alt: Algorithm: CLL with no active disease is observed; active disease is tested for del 17p/TP53 — intact goes to FCR (fit, under 70) or anti-CD20 plus chlorambucil or bendamustine (older/unfit); mutated goes to ibrutinib or idelalisib, with venetoclax second line.

blocks.text: **Ibrutinib** is oral and usually well tolerated, but it raises the risk of **atrial fibrillation**.

Sources disagree on first line. **Davidson 24e** (our authority) gives **FCR** for fit, TP53-intact patients under 70; Kumar still calls FCR first line for the young and fit. Newer US quick sources (Pocket Medicine, First Aid) prefer **BTK inhibitors or venetoclax-based** regimens even without TP53 loss. In exams, follow Davidson unless the question says otherwise — and remember that **TP53 loss steers treatment away from chemo-immunotherapy** in every source.

blocks.title: Complications of CLL
rows: Change to a high-grade lymphoma, usually **diffuse large B-cell lymphoma** (Hodgkin-like also occurs); poor prognosis
In about **10%**; IgG, active at 37 °C; strongly **DAT-positive**; treat with steroids
Anaemia with no erythroid precursors in the marrow; immunosuppression or chemotherapy
Acquired **hypogammaglobulinaemia** ± neutropenia; frequent chest and skin infections

blocks.text: **Richter’s transformation:** roughly **one case in two** arises from a new clone that is **unrelated to the original CLL**; such lymphomas behave like de novo DLBCL and respond similarly. **Clonally related** transformations do worse.
Frequency of Richter’s: **Davidson calls it rare**; Kumar gives **5–10%** and Pocket Medicine about **5%**. If asked for a figure, “around 5%, uncommon” fits all sources.
**Fludarabine** — part of FCR — is itself a drug cause of warm autoimmune haemolysis. New haemolysis during treatment may be due to the drug **or** to the CLL.

blocks.title: Related chronic B-cell disorders to tell apart
rows: CLL variant; older men; **massive splenomegaly**, little lymphadenopathy; WCC often > 400 × 10^9/L; large cells with a **prominent nucleolus**; very poor prognosis
Middle-aged men; splenomegaly, pancytopenia with **monocytopenia**; nodes uncommon; **CD25, CD103**, **BRAF** mutation; cladribine gives long remissions
CLL-type clone < 5 × 10^9/L, no nodal disease; observe

blocks.note: Look at: classification of haemolysis — CLL and fludarabine both appear among the secondary causes of warm autoimmune haemolysis.

blocks.text: CLL autoimmunity is **warm (IgG)**, not cold. Pair a CLL patient with **spherocytes and a strongly positive DAT** → warm AIHA.

cards.front: What is CLL in one line?
cards.back: A clonal expansion of small, mature-looking but functionally useless B lymphocytes.

cards.front: CLL vs SLL — what separates them?
cards.back: Same disease: CLL if the blood clone exceeds 5 × 10^9/L; SLL if mainly nodal with a lower blood count.

cards.front: CLL epidemiology: share of leukaemias, sex ratio, median age?
cards.back: About 30% of leukaemias (commonest); M:F 2:1; median age 65–70 years.

cards.front: Which population has strikingly little CLL?

cards.back: A CLL-type clone below 5 × 10^9/L; found in ~12% of healthy people; precedes nearly all CLL (like MGUS before myeloma).
Ibrutinib → BTK; idelalisib → PI3 kinase; venetoclax → BCL-2.
Incidentally — about 70% on a routine full blood count.
Monoclonal B cells CD19+, CD20+, CD23+ with aberrant CD5; single light chain (kappa or lambda).
Fragile CLL lymphocytes crushed while the film is made — an artefact but a classic CLL clue.

cards.front: Which test must be done before starting CLL treatment and why?
cards.back: FISH/mutation analysis for del 17p / TP53 — it decides between chemo-immunotherapy and BCR/BCL-2 inhibitors.
Anaemia and/or thrombocytopenia, regardless of how many lymphoid areas are enlarged (10% of patients).

cards.front: Rai stage II is defined by?
cards.back: Lymphocytosis plus splenomegaly, with or without lymphadenopathy (intermediate risk).

cards.front: Favourable vs adverse cytogenetics in CLL?
cards.back: Favourable: isolated del 13q, mutated IGHV. Adverse: del 11q (ATM), del 17p (TP53), unmutated IGHV.

cards.front: First-line treatment for a fit, TP53-intact CLL patient under 70 (Davidson)?

cards.back: Give pneumococcal, Hib and influenza; avoid live vaccines.
CLL turning into a high-grade lymphoma, usually DLBCL; uncommon (~5–10%) with poor prognosis.

cards.front: Type of AIHA seen in CLL?
cards.back: Warm (IgG) AIHA with a strongly positive DAT; about 10% of patients.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has rubbery, painless nodes in the neck and both axillae. Node biopsy shows a diffuse infiltrate of small lymphocytes that are CD5+ and CD23+. Her blood contains a matching clonal B-cell population of 1.2 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: The same cells as CLL, but the disease is mainly nodal and the blood clone is below 5 × 10^9/L — that is small lymphocytic lymphoma, the nodal form of the same disease.

items.stem: A well 58-year-old man has a pre-operative blood count with lymphocytes of 4.1 × 10^9/L. Flow cytometry finds a CD5+, CD23+ monoclonal B-cell population of 2.0 × 10^9/L. He has no nodes, no organomegaly, and normal haemoglobin and platelets.
items.explanation: A CLL-phenotype clone below 5 × 10^9/L with no nodal disease does not meet the criteria for CLL or SLL: this is monoclonal B lymphocytosis, managed by observation.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with CLL diagnosed 6 years ago has had three episodes of pneumonia this year. His neutrophil count is normal on each occasion and he has not received any treatment for CLL.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains his susceptibility to infection?
options: Failure of the clonal B cells to mature into antibody-secreting plasma cells
Loss of CD4 T cells caused by HTLV-1 infection
Hyperviscosity from a large IgM paraprotein
questions.explanation: CLL cells look mature but never become plasma cells, so normal antibody production falls (hypogammaglobulinaemia). With a normal neutrophil count, low immunoglobulins are the leading reason for recurrent bacterial chest infections.
whyNot: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma, not CLL, and nothing suggests it here.
Sequestration would lower the neutrophil count, which is normal.
Complement deficiency is not a recognised CLL mechanism in our sources.
Only about 5% of CLL patients have a monoclonal gammopathy, and hyperviscosity does not explain repeated pneumonia.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with CLL carrying a 17p deletion starts an oral drug that blocks a kinase in the B-cell receptor signalling pathway. Two months later she develops palpitations and an irregularly irregular pulse.
questions.leadIn: Which molecular target does her drug inhibit?
questions.explanation: An oral BCR-pathway kinase inhibitor used in TP53-disrupted CLL that causes atrial fibrillation is ibrutinib, which blocks Bruton’s tyrosine kinase.
whyNot: Idelalisib blocks PI3 kinase, but atrial fibrillation is the recognised hazard of ibrutinib.
BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein targeted by venetoclax, not a signalling kinase.
CD20 is a surface antigen targeted by antibodies such as rituximab, not a signalling kinase.
BCR-ABL is the target of imatinib in CML.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has had two chest infections and a cellulitis this year. She has painless nodes in both sides of the neck and a palpable spleen tip. WCC is 48 × 10^9/L, 90% small mature lymphocytes.
items.explanation: Older patient, recurrent infections, painless nodes, splenomegaly and a mature lymphocytosis well above 5 × 10^9/L: CLL.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has fatigue and recurrent infections. His spleen reaches the umbilicus but there are no palpable nodes. He has pancytopenia with a very low monocyte count, and the film shows lymphoid cells with fine cytoplasmic projections.
items.explanation: Like CLL it causes splenomegaly and infections, but nodes are rare, monocytes are low and the cells have hair-like projections: hairy cell leukaemia.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a lymphocyte count of 22 × 10^9/L on a routine blood count. The film shows small mature lymphocytes and many smudge cells. Haemoglobin and platelets are normal and he has no lymphadenopathy.
questions.leadIn: Which test will confirm the diagnosis?
options: Flow cytometric immunophenotyping of the blood
Excision biopsy of a lymph node
CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
questions.explanation: CLL is diagnosed on blood: a mature lymphocytosis above 5 × 10^9/L plus a monoclonal B-cell immunophenotype (CD5, CD19, CD23, one light chain). Flow cytometry is the most accurate test.
whyNot: Marrow examination is not needed to diagnose CLL; it is kept for difficult cases, prognosis and monitoring.
There are no nodes to biopsy, and the blood already holds the diagnostic cells.
CLL is staged clinically; imaging does not establish clonality.
An M protein is found in only about 5% and does not define CLL.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman has a lymphocytosis of 15 × 10^9/L. Flow cytometry is sent to distinguish CLL from other lymphoid disorders.
questions.leadIn: Which immunophenotype is most typical of CLL?
options: CD19+, CD23+, CD5+ B cells restricted to one light chain
CD19+ B cells, CD5− and CD23−, with both kappa and lambda light chains
CD138+ plasma cells with a single light chain
questions.explanation: CLL cells are monoclonal B cells (single kappa or lambda light chain) carrying CD19 and CD23 plus the aberrant T-cell antigen CD5.
whyNot: CD25 and CD103 are the markers of hairy cell leukaemia.
A mixed kappa/lambda population is polyclonal, which points to a reactive lymphocytosis.
CD34 with myeloperoxidase describes myeloid blasts (AML).
CD138+ clonal plasma cells point to a plasma-cell disorder such as myeloma.

questions.leadIn: Stage each patient using the system named in the stem. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: Using the Rai system: a 64-year-old man with CLL has palpable cervical and axillary nodes and a spleen 4 cm below the costal margin. Hb 135 g/L, platelets 210 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: Lymphocytosis plus splenomegaly (with or without nodes) and no cytopenia is Rai stage II.

items.stem: Using the Binet (Davidson clinical) system: a 77-year-old woman with CLL has a single enlarged inguinal node area. Hb is 95 g/L with a negative DAT and platelets are 85 × 10^9/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: she has only one lymphoid area, which might suggest stage A, but anaemia or thrombocytopenia places her in stage C whatever the node count.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old fit man with CLL has progressive stage B disease with drenching night sweats and weight loss. FISH shows no 17p deletion and TP53 is unmutated. He has no other illnesses.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Upfront myeloablative allogeneic stem cell transplant
Radiotherapy to involved node areas alone
questions.explanation: He needs treatment (B symptoms, progressive stage B). Fit, under 70 and TP53 intact: FCR is standard first-line care in Davidson.
whyNot: Systemic symptoms with progressive disease are an indication to treat, so watching is no longer appropriate.
Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML and has no role in CLL.
Transplant is only occasionally considered, with non-myeloablative conditioning, for fit high-risk patients.
Radiotherapy is for local problems from bulky nodes or spleen, not systemic disease with B symptoms.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old woman is found to have CLL on a routine blood count. She has one small cervical node, normal haemoglobin and platelets, and no symptoms. She is very anxious about having “leukaemia”.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Explain the indolent course and monitor the blood count every few months
questions.explanation: Stage A without progression needs no specific treatment and life expectancy is usually normal. Clear information, reassurance and periodic counts are the right approach.
whyNot: FCR is for active disease in fit patients; she has none of the triggers for treatment.
This regimen is for older patients who need treatment, which she does not yet.
Immunoglobulin replacement is for hypogammaglobulinaemia with recurrent infections.
Splenectomy is for autoimmune cytopenias, hypersplenism or massive splenomegaly.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man has had stable stage A CLL for 5 years. Over 6 weeks one neck node grows rapidly to 6 cm and he develops fevers and weight loss. Biopsy shows sheets of large B cells.
items.explanation: Rapid growth of one node with B symptoms and large-cell histology in long-standing CLL means transformation to a high-grade (DLBCL-type) lymphoma: Richter’s transformation.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with CLL becomes jaundiced; her haemoglobin falls from 128 to 78 g/L in 3 weeks. Reticulocytes are high, the film shows spherocytes and the DAT is strongly positive for IgG.
items.explanation: IgG-positive DAT with spherocytes and a brisk reticulocytosis is warm autoimmune haemolysis, the typical autoimmune complication of CLL.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: FISH for 17p deletion / TP53 mutation analysis
Bone marrow test for the Philadelphia chromosome
CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis

items.stem: A 67-year-old man has a lymphocyte count of 18 × 10^9/L and smudge cells on his film. His GP asks which test will show whether the lymphocytes are a single clone and confirm the diagnosis.
items.explanation: Clonality and the CD5/CD19/CD23 phenotype are shown by flow cytometry, the most accurate test for CLL.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with Binet stage C CLL is about to start treatment. Her haematologist needs the one result that decides between chemo-immunotherapy and a BTK inhibitor.
items.explanation: Del 17p / TP53 mutation predicts poor response to chemo-immunotherapy and directs therapy to ibrutinib-type drugs, so it must be checked before treatment starts.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with CLL has had four sinus and chest infections in a year despite a normal neutrophil count. His team wants to know whether immunoglobulin replacement could help.
items.explanation: Hypogammaglobulinaemia is common and progressive in CLL; measuring serum immunoglobulins shows whether replacement is justified.

items.stem: A 65-year-old woman with CLL develops jaundice and a falling haemoglobin. Which test shows antibody coating her red cells?
items.explanation: The direct antiglobulin test detects IgG (or complement) on red cells, confirming autoimmune haemolysis, a known CLL complication.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: An 81-year-old woman with heart failure and chronic kidney disease has progressive Binet stage C CLL. TP53 is intact. She is judged too frail for FCR.
items.explanation: Older, less fit patients get an anti-CD20 antibody with gentle chemotherapy; obinutuzumab plus chlorambucil gives better responses than rituximab plus chlorambucil.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with CLL now has progressive lymphadenopathy and falling platelets. FISH shows a 17p deletion.
items.explanation: Two steps: he needs treatment (progression, cytopenia), and del 17p means poor response to chemo-immunotherapy, so a BTK inhibitor (ibrutinib) is chosen.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with stable, otherwise untreated CLL develops warm autoimmune haemolysis with a haemoglobin of 80 g/L.
items.explanation: First-line treatment of haemolysis in CLL is with steroids; chemotherapy is added if it responds poorly.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman with 17p-deleted CLL progresses after a year on ibrutinib. Her team chooses an oral drug that blocks an anti-apoptotic protein.
items.explanation: Venetoclax inhibits BCL-2 and is the second-line option after a BTK inhibitor in TP53-disrupted disease.

questions.theme: Causes of a raised lymphocyte count
questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had 3 weeks of coughing fits ending in a whoop. Lymphocytes are 9 × 10^9/L; flow cytometry shows a mixed (polyclonal) population of B and T cells.
items.explanation: Step 1: the lymphocytosis is polyclonal, so it is reactive, not a clonal neoplasm. Step 2: a paroxysmal whooping cough points to Bordetella pertussis, a classic bacterial cause of lymphocytosis.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man has a spleen filling the left abdomen but almost no palpable nodes. WCC is 450 × 10^9/L; most cells are large lymphocytes with a prominent nucleolus.
items.explanation: Step 1: a B-cell picture in an older man resembles CLL. Step 2: massive spleen, little lymphadenopathy, WCC above 400 and nucleolated large cells are the hallmarks of prolymphocytic leukaemia, a CLL variant with a very poor prognosis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has lymphocytes of 3.8 × 10^9/L. Flow cytometry shows a CD5+, CD23+ monoclonal B-cell clone of 1.1 × 10^9/L. Examination is normal.
items.explanation: Step 1: the phenotype is that of CLL. Step 2: the clone is below 5 × 10^9/L and there is no nodal disease, so the CLL and SLL criteria are not met. Step 3: this is monoclonal B lymphocytosis; at above 0.5 × 10^9/L it counts as high-count MBL and deserves at least yearly review.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old fit man with CLL has cervical, axillary and inguinal nodes. Hb is 92 g/L (DAT negative, reticulocytes low) and platelets are 80 × 10^9/L. FISH shows a 17p deletion.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Step 1 — stage: anaemia and thrombocytopenia make this stage C. Step 2 — the cytopenias are not autoimmune (DAT negative, low reticulocytes), so this is marrow failure, an indication to treat. Step 3 — the 17p deletion (TP53 loss) predicts a poor response to chemo-immunotherapy, so a B-cell receptor pathway inhibitor is used: ibrutinib, the oral BTK inhibitor (watch for atrial fibrillation).
whyNot: FCR is standard only for fit patients without TP53 disruption; 17p-deleted disease responds poorly to it.
Chemotherapy is again ineffective with TP53 loss, and chlorambucil is a gentle option for the unfit.
Marrow failure with stage C disease needs treatment now.
Splenectomy is for autoimmune cytopenias or hypersplenism, not marrow infiltration.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed CLL has a FISH abnormality that, if he needs treatment, makes ibrutinib rather than fludarabine-based chemo-immunotherapy the preferred choice.
items.explanation: Two steps: the abnormality that redirects first-line therapy from FCR to a BTK inhibitor is TP53 disruption; on FISH this is loss of 17p, where TP53 sits. These patients respond poorly to chemo-immunotherapy, so ibrutinib is offered.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with CLL has FISH showing loss of the region carrying the ATM tumour suppressor gene. Her disease is expected to evolve quickly.
items.explanation: ATM lies on 11q; del 11q is an adverse marker linked to a rapidly evolving course.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with stage A CLL has a molecular result associated with a median survival of more than 20 years.
items.explanation: Somatically mutated IGHV predicts an indolent course (median survival > 20 years versus about 8 years when unmutated).

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with CLL has FISH using a chromosome 12 centromere probe that shows three signals per nucleus. Her haematologist calls this finding prognostically neutral.
items.explanation: Three chromosome 12 signals means trisomy 12, regarded as a neutral marker.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man with CLL has a haemoglobin of 70 g/L with an almost absent reticulocyte count. The DAT is negative. His marrow shows a modest lymphocytic infiltrate, normal white cell and platelet precursors, but no red cell precursors at all.
items.explanation: Two steps: low reticulocytes mean under-production, not haemolysis; selective absence of erythroid precursors with other lines intact is pure red cell aplasia, which is associated with CLL.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with stable CLL presents with bruising. Her platelet count is 12 × 10^9/L; haemoglobin, neutrophils and spleen size are unchanged from last year.
items.explanation: An isolated, sudden fall in platelets with other lines intact and no marrow failure suggests immune thrombocytopenia; CLL is a recognised secondary cause of ITP.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man with CLL has a spleen extending into the pelvis and falling counts of all three cell lines. DAT is negative and marrow infiltration is only moderate. His counts recover after splenectomy.
items.explanation: Pooling and destruction of cells in a massive spleen (hypersplenism) lowers all counts and is one reason for splenectomy in CLL.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with CLL has a haemoglobin of 88 g/L and platelets of 60 × 10^9/L, both falling steadily over a year. Reticulocytes are low and the DAT is negative. His spleen is only just palpable, and a trephine shows the marrow diffusely replaced by small lymphocytes.
items.explanation: Two steps: low reticulocytes with a negative DAT mean under-production, not haemolysis; two lines falling together with a marrow packed by CLL cells (rather than a selective loss of red cell precursors) is marrow failure from infiltration, which is treated with chemotherapy (and transfusion when needed).

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has stage A CLL under observation. Over the past 4 months his lymphocyte count has risen from 20 to 45 × 10^9/L. He feels well.
questions.leadIn: Which finding in this situation is an indication to start treatment?
options: The lymphocyte count has more than doubled in under 6 months
Smudge cells are present on the film
A single 1.5 cm cervical node is palpable
questions.explanation: A rapidly rising lymphocyte count — doubling in less than 6 months — marks progressive disease and is an indication for treatment.
whyNot: This is only the diagnostic threshold and does not by itself require treatment.
Smudge cells are a film artefact, not a marker of activity.
Isolated del 13q is a favourable marker.
A small single node fits stage A and is not a reason to treat.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has been on ibrutinib for 3 months for TP53-mutated CLL. She now has palpitations and breathlessness on exertion; her pulse is irregularly irregular at 130/min.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Atrial fibrillation provoked by the drug
questions.explanation: Ibrutinib is usually well tolerated but raises the risk of atrial fibrillation, which fits an irregularly irregular tachycardia.
whyNot: Richter’s presents with rapid node growth and systemic symptoms, not an arrhythmia.
Haemolysis may cause breathlessness but not an irregularly irregular pulse.
Low immunoglobulins cause infections, not arrhythmia.
Pneumocystis causes breathlessness and hypoxia, but not an irregularly irregular pulse.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with CLL is planning travel and asks which vaccines he can safely have.
questions.leadIn: Which vaccine type should he avoid?
questions.explanation: Immunosuppressed CLL patients should not receive live vaccines; pneumococcal, Hib and influenza vaccination are recommended.
whyNot: Pneumococcal vaccination is specifically recommended in CLL.
Hib vaccination is specifically recommended in CLL.
Influenza vaccination is recommended; the inactivated vaccine is not live.
A toxoid is not a live vaccine, so it carries no risk of vaccine-strain infection.

questions.leadIn: Match each patient below with the single best option from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has a spleen palpable 12 cm below the costal margin. WCC is 180 × 10^9/L with neutrophils and myelocytes predominating, a basophilia and fewer than 10% blasts.
items.explanation: A granulocytosis with the full range of precursors, basophilia and few blasts is chronic myeloid leukaemia — the opposite of the lymphocytosis of CLL.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman has lymphocytes of 40 × 10^9/L, small and mature with smudge cells, that are CD5+ and CD23+. Electrophoresis shows a small monoclonal band; there are no bone lesions and calcium is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: the blood picture and phenotype are CLL; the small M band does not mean myeloma because about 5% of CLL patients have a monoclonal gammopathy.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has pancytopenia with marked monocytopenia and splenomegaly but no lymphadenopathy. Flow cytometry shows B cells expressing CD25 and CD103, and a BRAF mutation is found.
items.explanation: CD25 and CD103 positivity, a BRAF mutation, monocytopenia and splenomegaly without nodes describe hairy cell leukaemia.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with CLL. She has enlarged nodes in the neck only, Hb 140 g/L and platelets 220 × 10^9/L. She asks what the future holds.
questions.leadIn: Which statement best describes her outlook?
options: She will probably have a normal life expectancy and may never need treatment
She needs FCR now to prevent progression
Her median survival is about 2 years
Her CLL will inevitably transform into high-grade lymphoma
questions.explanation: This is clinical stage A. Most stage A patients have a normal life expectancy, and about 30% of all CLL patients never need treatment.
whyNot: Early-stage disease is managed expectantly; early treatment is not given.
Median survival in CLL overall is about 10 years, and longer in stage A.
Chlorambucil is palliative; CLL is incurable without allogeneic transplant.
Richter’s transformation is uncommon (about 5–10%).

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has had CLL for 8 years. Over 2 months he has developed a rapidly growing abdominal mass, fevers and weight loss. Biopsy of the mass shows sheets of large B cells.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rapid nodal growth with systemic symptoms and large B cells on biopsy in long-standing CLL is Richter’s transformation, usually to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
whyNot: PLL shows a very high count of nucleolated prolymphocytes with massive splenomegaly, not a large-cell nodal mass.
Hairy cell leukaemia is a separate disorder with splenomegaly, pancytopenia and few nodes.
MBL is a small clone without nodal disease.
Pure red cell aplasia causes isolated anaemia, not a mass.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is referred with an incidental lymphocytosis. She asks whether she was exposed to something that caused it.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about the aetiology of CLL is most accurate?
options: No specific cause is identified in most patients
It is caused mainly by previous alkylating chemotherapy
It is caused by HTLV-1 infection
It usually follows atomic-bomb radiation exposure
It is a direct result of Down’s syndrome
questions.explanation: The cause of leukaemia is unknown in most patients and our sources give no CLL-specific environmental cause. Nearly all CLL arises from a pre-existing monoclonal B lymphocytosis.
whyNot: Alkylating agents are linked mainly to myeloid leukaemia after a latent period.
HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
Radiation after the atomic bombings was linked to myeloid leukaemia.
Down’s syndrome is listed only as a general leukaemia risk factor, not a recognised cause of CLL.

ospe.identify: Blood film: many small mature lymphocytes with **smudge cells** → chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
FISH panel A (green 17p probe, red 11q probe): 17p signal lost while 11q is normal → **17p (TP53) deletion**, the adverse marker that steers treatment away from chemo-immunotherapy.
FISH panel B: three chromosome 12 centromere signals → **trisomy 12**, a neutral prognostic finding in CLL.
Lymphoid cells with hair-like cytoplasmic projections → **hairy cell leukaemia**, the main CLL look-alike (splenomegaly, few nodes).
